So the current pair passes over three separate disguises of the exact failure Task 8 exists for, and the anchored, chromium-scoped pair catches all three while staying green on the healthy config. The slice I used is the ci.yml idiom the finding points at: `config.split(/^\s+name: 'chromium',$/m)[1]?.split(/^\s+\},$/m)[0] ?? ''` — the terminator matches the entry's own closing `    },` and not the `use: { … },` line above it, because that line has content before the brace. One tightening the spike produced: the `name:` half is best expressed as `assert.ok(chromium, 'the chromium project is gone — the shots never run')` on the slice itself, which keeps Task 8 Step 4 arm 3's quoted message intact; a separate `assert.match` on the name line would be redundant with the slice succeeding.
F-10.scenario: Someone is chasing a screenshot failure and, to get the build past it for an hour, comments out the one line that tells the screenshot lane which files to photograph and drops in a different one. They mean to put it back. The build goes green — properly green, not skipped — so the reminder never arrives and the line stays commented for months. The lane still blocks merges, still runs, still reports success, and photographs nothing at all. The check written specifically to make that impossible looks at the file, finds the old line sitting there behind its two slashes, and counts it.
F-10.whats_wrong: Task 8 Step 2's last two assertions (lines 1655-1656) search the whole config text with no line anchor and no scoping to the `chromium` entry: `assert.match(config, /name:\s*'chromium'/, …)` and `assert.match(config, /testMatch:\s*'\*\*\/\*\.vr\.ts'/, …)`. Measured, both stay green over a config whose real `testMatch` line is commented out and replaced, over one whose `name: 'chromium'` line is commented out and renamed, and over one where the two projects' patterns have been swapped — leaving an unscoped CI run at exit 0 over zero pixels, the failure this task's opening paragraph describes. Every other assertion in the same suite is anchored to a real line (`/^\s+run: …$/m` at line 1880, `/^\s+container: …$/m` at line 1892, `/^IMAGE=…$/gm` at line 687) and the plan states the reason at line 1877: the unanchored form survives a commented-out line.
F-10.proposed_fix: Slice the config down to the `chromium` project entry — split on an anchored `name: 'chromium',` line and stop at that entry's own closing `},`, the way Task 9's web-job test slices ci.yml — then assert inside the slice with an anchored `/^\s+testMatch: '\*\*\/\*\.vr\.ts',$/m`. Keep the message `the chromium project is gone — the shots never run` on the `assert.ok` that tests the slice, so Task 8 Step 4 arm 3's quoted expectation still holds. Add a comment naming the three disguises the anchoring closes, since that is the reasoning the plan already writes down for its other anchored assertions.
F-10.why_it_works: All four states were run, not argued. The anchored, scoped pair is green on the healthy config and red on each of the three disguises the current pair sleeps through — a commented-out and replaced `testMatch`, a commented-out and renamed project, and the two projects' patterns swapped. The scoping is what catches the swap specifically: the `e2e` entry sits above the slice, so a `'**/*.vr.ts'` that lands on it is simply not in the text being searched. The anchoring is what catches the commented-out lines, which is the exact argument the plan already makes at line 1877 for the run-line assertion. And the repo's own Prettier leaves this config byte-identical, so the anchors are not fighting the formatter.

F-10.severity_rationale: P2 is right. On the day this lands the config is correct and both forms pass, so it is not the P1 class of a check that cannot fail today. But this pair of assertions is the last line of the one test written to stop a merge-blocking gate reading green over zero pixels — the failure the task's own opening paragraph spends five lines describing — and it was measured to survive three different ways of causing exactly that. It also breaks the suite's own rule: every other assertion here is anchored, and the plan states the reason. The fix costs four lines and was verified green on the formatted config.

F-13.contradicts: Checked what the strip touches and what depends on it. (1) NO ARM BREAKS. I ran every arm of the guard over the real assembled shot file both raw and stripped: healthy passes both ways. The four surface anchors, the `backgroundColor` read and the `failOnUnexpectedPageErrors()` call all survive the strip because each has a real code occurrence, which I counted (`(page, 'player-rail')` 1/1, `(page, 'transport-row')` 1/1, `var(--destructive)` 1/1, `backgroundColor` 8/8, `failOnUnexpectedPageErrors()` 1/1). (2) THE STRIP SILENTLY FIXES A LIVE SECOND HOLE, which is a point in its favour and which the finding did not claim — see the spike. (3) COMPANION EDITS: Task 8 Step 4 needs a new arm (comment out one shot, expect the pairing message); its heading still reads 'Four separate checks' (line 1670) while listing six, so it should be renumbered while the arm is added — that staleness is pre-existing, from lap 2, not caused here. (4) The guard's own comment at line 1576-1579 explains that the trailing `\(` on the skip pattern is what stops it matching 'any prose occurrence, a snapshot filename, or a commented-out line'; with the strip in place the commented-out third of that sentence is handled by the strip instead, so the comment should be reworded rather than left claiming a job it no longer does alone. (5) NO COLLISION with F-10, which edits the same Step 2 block: F-10 acts on `config`, this acts on `sources`, and the strip is deliberately not applied to the config (F-10's anchors do that work). (6) NO COLLISION with F-1, whose added expectations are real code and survive the strip. (7) The `\.png` anchor and its comment (lines 1598-1600) are untouched.
F-13.spike:
RAN the guard for real over a shot file assembled from the plan's own code blocks, and the finding HELD — plus I found a second, LIVE hole by running it. I concatenated the ts blocks from Task 4 Step 3, Task 5 Steps 3-4, Task 6 Steps 1-3 and Task 7 Steps 1-2 into a 349-line `pages.vr.ts` (nine shots: landing, player-bundled-beat, player-long-score, player-transport-pressed, player-rail-ghost-hover, player-header-tooltip, player-narrow, player-skeleton, player-engine-error — matching Task 7 Step 5's list exactly), wrote the nine matching `-chromium-linux.png` baselines, and ran every arm of Task 8's guard as written and with F-13's `code()` strip:
  healthy (control)                             AS WRITTEN passes    WITH STRIP passes  (9 shots both ways)
  one toHaveScreenshot line commented with //   AS WRITTEN PASSES    WITH STRIP fails, 'the shots and the committed -chromium-linux baselines no longer pair up'  (8 shots)
  the narrow shot block-commented /* */         AS WRITTEN PASSES    WITH STRIP fails, same message                                                              (8 shots)
  one toHaveScreenshot call DELETED (Step 4 arm 6) both fail       — so the plan's documented bite-proof still works unchanged
THE SPIKE FOUND A SECOND HOLE THE FIX ALSO CLOSES, and it is live in the document today. `var(--elevate)` occurs TWICE in the assembled file — once as the real probe line in Task 6 Step 1, and once inside Task 7 Step 2's comment ('The throwaway probe is how Task 6's ghost hover resolves `var(--elevate)`', added by lap 2). I deleted the real probe line and re-ran: the anchor `/var\(--elevate\)/` still matched the surviving COMMENT, so the guard stayed green over a deleted surface assertion — precisely the trap Task 8's own comment claims it avoided ('an id substring stays green on a deleted assertion'). With the strip, the same deletion fails the guard. So one of the four surface anchors is already defeatable as the document stands, and this one fix closes both holes. SAFETY CHECKED: the assembled file's only block comments are four JSDoc `/** … */` blocks, and no string or regex literal contains `/*` or a line starting with `//`, so the strip removes 42 comment lines and nothing else. It is a heuristic, not a parser, and the `after` says so.
F-13.scenario: Someone needs one screenshot out of the way for an afternoon — it keeps failing on a change they are still working on — so they put two slashes in front of it rather than deleting anything, meaning to take them out later. They forget. The lane now photographs eight screens and calls it nine; the reference image for the ninth sits in the folder, unused, pairing up with a line of code that no longer runs. The guard written precisely to notice that the lane has stopped comparing something reads the commented-out line as if it were live, matches it to the leftover image, and reports that everything pairs up. Every check is green and one screen has quietly stopped being watched.
F-13.whats_wrong: Task 8 Step 2 derives shot names by text-matching `toHaveScreenshot\('([^']+\.png)'` across the RAW source (lines 1601-1607), so a `//`-prefixed or block-commented call still counts and still pairs with its on-disk baseline. Measured, both disguises leave the merge-blocking gate green over eight shots instead of nine. The only disable routes the guard checks are `test.skip` and `test.fixme` (line 1580-1584), and neither is present in a commented-out shot. Step 4's bite-proof only ever deletes a call outright (arm 6, line 1681), so the hole is never exercised. The same raw-text reading defeats a surface anchor today: `var(--elevate)` appears both in Task 6 Step 1's real probe line and in Task 7 Step 2's comment, so deleting the probe leaves the anchor matching the comment.
F-13.proposed_fix: Strip comments once, at the point `sources` is built, rather than threading a `code(source)` call through each assertion — every content match below then reads the stripped text and no arm can be forgotten. Add a seventh arm to Task 8 Step 4 that comments out one shot with `//` and expects the pairing message, and renumber that step's heading, which says 'Four separate checks' over six items. Reword the skip-pattern comment, whose third clause (the trailing `\(` guarding against 'a commented-out line') is handled by the strip once it lands. Leave the config assertions reading the raw config — anchoring, not stripping, is the right tool there.
F-13.why_it_works: Measured over a shot file assembled from the plan's own nine code blocks with its own nine baseline names. As written, the guard passes over a `//`-commented shot and over a block-commented one; with the strip it fails on both with the pairing message the plan already writes. Both forms still fail on the plan's existing arm 6 (a deleted call), so nothing documented breaks. The healthy file passes both ways and every other arm survives the strip, which I verified by counting each anchor's occurrences before and after — each has a real code occurrence, so none of them was living in a comment. And the strip closes a hole that exists today rather than only a hypothetical one: with the real `--elevate` probe deleted, the anchor still matched Task 7's comment and the guard stayed green; stripped, it goes red.

F-13.severity_rationale: P2 is right, at the very top of the band, and I considered raising it. Nothing is broken on the day this lands — all nine shots run and all nine pair — so it is not the P1 class. What pushes it to the top of P2 is that the spike found the hole is not only about future commenting-out: one of the four surface anchors is ALREADY defeatable in the document as it stands, because lap 2's own comment repeated `var(--elevate)`, so deleting that surface assertion leaves the guard green today. That is a named Review Focus failure mode ('One of the four surface assertions dropped') whose guard does not currently hold for one of the four. It stays P2 because it still takes a second action — someone deleting or parking something — to turn it into a real loss, and the fix is three lines plus one bite-proof arm.
